content.text:
To reach universal energy access and climate goals, we need to completely reimagine how energy is produced, distributed, and used.

The energy system we need is:
Where We Need to Go: Building a Just and Climate-Aligned Energy System

The next decade is decisive. Infrastructure decisions made today will shape the lives of generations to come. So what must we do?

Position decentralized renewables as core development infrastructure, not just a climate solution.

Scale up digital, data, and AI to improve access, efficiency, and equity in energy systems.

Close the finance gap by building pipelines of bankable projects that deliver multiple benefits from powering rural clinics and schools to preserving biodiversity and boosting food systems.

Align public policy, regulation, and private capital toward inclusive, climate-compatible energy futures.
How Do We Get There

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: energy for development
concepts.body: Energy for development refers to the provision and use of energy resources to support economic growth, improve living standards, and enhance social well-being in communities, particularly in developing regions.

concepts.title: energy trilemma
concepts.body: The energy trilemma refers to the challenge of balancing three key objectives in energy policy: ensuring energy security, promoting environmental sustainability, and providing energy equity or affordability for all consumers.

concepts.title: paris agreement goals
concepts.body: The Paris Agreement goals refer to the international commitments made by countries to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and to enhance the ability to adapt to climate change impacts.

content.quote: Achieving universal energy access and net zero emissions by 2050 will require nothing short of the complete transformation of the global energy system.

content.text:
As we have learned in this lesson, a just energy transition is not just a technical challenge. It’s a question of power, values, and urgency. The energy transition will not succeed unless it works for everyone, especially those historically left behind.

In the rest of the module, we’ll dive deeper into how we got here, what needs to change, and we can lead the charge toward a just, inclusive, and sustainable energy future.

Faced with the dual challenge of balancing universal, affordable access with climate mitigation, the world is slowly starting to shift energy systems.

The cost of solar electricity has dropped by over 85% between 2010 and 2020 (IRENA, 2022), and renewables are now the cheapest source of new power in most of the world. In 2024, clean energy investments reached a historic $2 trillion, more than doubling since 2020 (IEA, 2024). As illustrated in the following chart, the share of renewable energy in global electricity generation has already risen from approximately 20% in 2000 to over 30% in 2023. Looking ahead, it is projected to increase by an additional 90% by 2030, compared to 2023 levels.

Solar and wind are finally outcompeting coal and gas in many markets. For the first time, renewables are set to become the largest source of global electricity.

Governments, companies, and communities around the world are increasingly committing to net-zero pathways. Breakthroughs in battery storage, green hydrogen, and energy access solutions offer hope. These are signs of genuine transformation.

But is it happening fast enough?
Progress: Clean energy is accelerating

content.text:
For decades, fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas have been the primary sources of energy for electricity, transportation, and industrial processes.

Since 1950, fossil fuel consumption has surged—growing eightfold—and has nearly doubled since 1980. While coal use has declined in many regions, oil and gas consumption continues to rise rapidly.

However, these energy practices raise several concerns:
Despite some progress, the underlying energy system is still structurally unjust, carbon-heavy, and deeply unequal.
Paradox: Fossil Fuel are still predominant

The dual challenge of expanding energy access and addressing climate change, the twin imperatives of sustainable energy, is at the heart of the development agenda.

 Energy is essential for economic growth, education, healthcare, and broader human development. Yet, the way the world has historically powered development—through fossil fuels—is now destabilizing the climate and putting those very development gains at risk.

Emerging economies are rightly seeking to grow, industrialize, and prosper. But if this growth follows the same fossil-fueled path of the past, climate goals will collapse and the poorest will once again suffer the most.

So we face a tricky equation: the same systems that deny energy to the poor are also destabilizing the climate.
This also raises urgent questions:

Who gets to industrialize, and how?

Can the right to develop be realized without deepening the climate crisis?

And can we build a new energy system that both powers prosperity and protects the planet?

The answers lie in reimagining development not as a trade-off between growth and sustainability, but as a transformational opportunity to leapfrog into cleaner, more resilient energy systems that are aligned with climate goals and grounded in justice.
Energy also Powers Climate Change

The very fuel that powered industrial development is now accelerating a global crisis. Fossil fuels—coal, oil, and gas—still make up more the majority of the world’s energy supply, despite decades of climate warnings. As a result, energy production and use now account for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions due to the combustion of fossil fuels for electricity, heat, and transport.

This presents a significant challenge for sustainable development, as the impacts of climate change, such as extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and shifting agricultural patterns, undermine economic stability, food security, and public health.

These effects disproportionately affect the poorest and most vulnerable populations, who are least equipped to adapt and have contributed the least to global emissions. As a result, climate change exacerbates existing inequalities and poses a direct threat to development gains, particularly in low-income and climate-vulnerable countries.

To better understand this relationship, we often look at the Human Development Index (HDI), a measure that gives us a snapshot of a nation's overall well-being. The HDI is a composite indicator consisting of life expectancy, education and per capita income indicators. Countries are scored between 0 and 1, with higher scores reflecting greater development.
Energy Powers Development

Energy consumption is closely tied to HDI. At low levels of development, even small increases in energy use lead to significant improvements in HDI. However, as development increases, additional energy use has diminishing returns, with smaller improvements in HDI at higher levels of energy consumption. While the relationship falls apart at very high levels of HDI, understanding this connection is crucial for sustainable growth.

content.title: The Great Energy Dilemma: Paradoxes of Sustainable Development
content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

Energy represent both an immense opportunity for development and a challenge for preserving life on Earth.

It powers the lights in our homes, the machines in our hospitals, and the growth of entire economies. Yet the way we have produced and consumed energy, overwhelmingly through fossil fuels, has created major environmental and climate issue that endanger opportunities for development.

This is the great energy dilemma of our time: we must expand energy access to lift billions out of poverty while simultaneously slashing emissions to preserve a livable planet.

Can we do both urgently, equitably, and at scale?

This lesson unpacks the twin imperatives of development and climate action, and the deep contradictions they expose in today’s energy system.

Why does the Global South, rich in renewable potential, receive only a sliver of clean energy investment?

How can we justify a world where the same fossil-fueled growth model that built wealth for some now threatens the survival of others?


We invite you to explore these paradoxes that will shape the future of humanity. This lesson challenges you to think beyond false choices, between growth and sustainability, between rich and poor, between climate goals and development rights, and toward an energy transition that is just, inclusive, and transformative.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: Part 1: Development and Climate: The Twin Imperatives

content.text:
We live in a world shaped—and strained—by energy.
On the one hand, energy is the lifeblood of development: powering homes, schools, hospitals, economies. On the other, the way we produce and use energy is damaging our planet and ecosystems, threatening the very foundations of life itself.

This is the defining paradox of our time. We need more energy to ensure every person can live a dignified, healthy life. But we also need cleaner energy immediately to avert catastrophic climate change. These two goals are both non-negotiable. Yet they are pulling against each other in a world still structured by deep inequalities, outdated infrastructure, and powerful fossil fuel interests.


The paradox of sustainable development lies on these two main elements that are indissociable from each other and critical to understand the most significant challenges of our times.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: Part 2: Progress and Paradoxes in the Push for Just Energy Transitions

content.text: Part 2 Overview

The global energy transition is gaining momentum, but beneath the surface of progress lies a series contradiction.

Solar and wind are breaking records. Clean technologies are cheaper and spreading faster than ever before.

And yet, fossil fuels remain deeply entrenched, access remains deeply unequal, and investment flows continue to bypass the communities that need them most.

Are we truly transitioning or just rearranging the imbalance? Why is clean energy booming while fossil fuels still dominate? These questions are crucial to frame the issue of energy for development and question the systems at play in its transformation.

content.title:
Africa, is home to 20% of the world’s population, and 80% of all people lacking electricity access,
Yet the continent receives just under 2% of global clean energy investment, despite vast solar and wind resources.

Global investments in the energy transition reached a record $2 trillion in 2024.
Yet fossil fuel subsidies exceeded $620 billion in 2023 (IEA, 2024).

content.text:
The challenge of a just energy transition has dual imperatives, and multiple contradictions. How do we move beyond the current structure and build a system that is beneficial for people, planet and prosperity?

This section explores the foundational shifts required to transition from today’s outdated, fossil-fueled energy systems to a future that is clean, inclusive, and climate-aligned. It begins by diagnosing the limitations of our current centralized energy model, one that disproportionately benefits the wealthy, remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, and suffers from significant inefficiencies and sectoral vulnerabilities.
It then presents the energy system we need: one that is renewable, non-polluting, and designed to deliver cross-sectoral development gains, from health and education to food security and resilience.

Finally, it outlines key levers for transformative change in the coming decade. This section sets the stage for understanding that the energy transition is not just a technological upgrade, it is a political, social, and moral imperative.

content.title: Energy as a Driver for Development
content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

Energy powers our world—from homes and hospitals to industries and digital systems. It is the backbone of modern life, essential for delivering critical social services such as healthcare, education, water supply, heating, and cooling. But energy is not just about convenience—it shapes living standards, economic opportunity, public safety, and resilience.

Yet access alone is not enough. Today, 1.18 billion people live in energy poverty, lacking the adequate, reliable, and affordable energy needed for lighting, cooking, communication, and daily life. To unlock human potential and drive sustainable development, we need energy systems that are not only available—but reliable, inclusive, and resilient—systems that uphold basic rights, enable access to clean water and sanitation, and strengthen community safety and well-being.

As we have seen previously, energy plays a crucial role in achieving prosperity, and as societies grow and thrive, their dependence on energy and the services it provides increases significantly. However, this pursuit of economic growth, especially through increased fossil fuel consumption, often comes at a cost to the environment. The energy trilemma—balancing energy security, equity, and sustainability—captures these complex trade-offs between energy production, economic advancement, and state of environment.

This trilemma is not just an abstract concept; it is deeply intertwined with issues of fairness and equity. Developing countries and regions reliant on fossil fuels often face a difficult balancing act: ensuring reliable energy access (security), maintaining affordable prices (equity), and advancing environmental protection (sustainability).

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: A: Energy Consumption Disparities

content.text:
Significant disparities exist globally in energy use, prosperity, health, political influence, and resource demands.

Global energy use remains deeply unequal—reflecting broader disparities in wealth, health, political influence, and resource consumption. Per capita energy consumption underscores the scale of this divide. An average American, for example, uses 12 times more energy than an average Indian—consuming in one month what an Indian uses in an entire year. The gap is even wider between North America and Africa, where the average North American consumes over 50 times more energy than the average African. Even among middle-income countries, stark contrasts remain.

These disparities highlight not only differences in income and infrastructure—but also unequal access to the many benefits energy enables, from healthcare and education to mobility, productivity, and climate resilience.
For comparison, common household appliances consume:

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: B: Energy Use and Climate Change

content.text:
Energy consumption has surged due to population growth, industrialization, globalization, rising per capita demand and overall economic growth.

Consequently, the heavy reliance on fossil fuels has made the energy sector the primary contributor to climate change, while also significantly impacting environmental quality and public health.

Climate change, at its core, is largely an energy issue, with about 75% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions coming from energy use.

Reaching net zero emissions targets requires both an energy transition and approaches that “leapfrog” historic energy development pathways. The biggest sources of emissions within the energy sector are electricity and heat generation, followed by transportation and manufacturing. Figure 5 illustrates historical trends and annual variations in global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from energy combustion and industrial processes, providing a clear picture of how energy consumption impacts climate change.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: C: Inefficiencies in the Global Energy System

content.text:
The current global energy system operates at only 37% efficiency (RMI, 2019), meaning that nearly two-thirds of the primary energy produced is lost due to inefficiencies in generation, transportation, and end-use.

In 2019, about 33% of the energy produced globally was lost before even reaching consumers, due to production and transportation inefficiencies. Another 30% was wasted on the demand side, as energy was converted into useful energy (see Figure 7).

More specifically, most energy losses come from inefficiencies in fossil fuel production and delivery (177 EJ/year), transportation (19 EJ/year), and usage (183 EJ/year). Fossil fuel power plants and internal combustion engines account for nearly half of global energy waste, alongside significant losses from the underutilization of byproducts and waste heat.

Wasting 379 EJ of energy each year results in a loss of approximately $4.6 trillion globally—$1 trillion on the supply side and $3.6 trillion on the demand side.

This equates to 40% of global energy spending and 5% of global GDP, which is roughly double the annual investments in the energy system.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: D: Challenges to Energy Security in a Fossil Fuel-dependent World

content.text:
The challenges of relying on fossil fuels for energy security are less about the resources themselves and more about external factors like geopolitics, social, economics, and the environment.

Many major fossil fuel-exporting countries often face political instability, which can disrupt the supply of oil, gas, and coal. For low-income countries that rely heavily on fuel imports, these disruptions can lead to energy shortages, economic stress, and reduced access to basic services. Fossil fuels also depend on complex supply chains—pipelines, shipping routes, and refineries—that are vulnerable to conflicts, accidents, and natural disasters.

In addition, global events such as wars, natural disasters, sanctions, or economic crises can cause energy prices to fluctuate, making them unpredictable. For resource-rich but low-income nations, fossil fuel exports can provide economic stability, yet they also expose them to market volatility and the "resource curse," where wealth from fuel exports does not translate into broader economic development. This volatility strains international relations as countries compete to secure affordable energy supplies.

Moreover, producing fossil fuels does not always guarantee energy security for a country, and it can lead to unequal distribution of resources, where not all citizens benefit equally from the profits or energy generated. In short, fossil fuels present significant risks to a stable and secure energy supply, largely due to external geopolitical and economic factors.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: E. Rising Global Energy Demand

content.text:
As economies grow, especially in developing countries, energy demand rises.

Global energy consumption is expected to increase by 15% by 2050, driven by population growth, economic development, and the expanding use of electricity across sectors. While developed countries may see a 10% reduction in energy use due to efficiency improvements, energy demand in developing countries is projected to grow by over 25% because more people are getting lifted out of energy povertyhh.
